tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Maya has finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday.
Our hiking club has met every Saturday since April.
While the band was rehearsing, the lights suddenly went out.
Leo used to swimming before school every morning.
By next Friday, the volunteers will plant fifty saplings.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — A finished time marker such as "last Tuesday" calls for past simple ("finished"), not present perfect.

Tip: Spot calendar anchors (yesterday, last week, in 2019) — they usually kill present perfect.

TRUE — Present perfect with "since" correctly signals a habit that began in the past and continues now.

Tip: Pair "since + starting point" with present perfect, not past simple.

TRUE — Past continuous sets the background rehearsal; past simple marks the sudden blackout.

Tip: Longer background → continuous; shorter interrupt → simple past.

FALSE — Past habit needs "used to" + base verb: "used to swim," not "used to swimming."

Tip: "Used to" + V1 for habits; "be used to" + -ing for familiarity.

FALSE — Completion before next Friday needs future perfect: "will have planted," not plain "will plant."

Tip: "By + future time" often flags future perfect.
tasks.solution_overview: Warm up on classic tense traps: finished time versus "since," background continuous versus a short interrupt, "used to" form, and future perfect with "by." Read each verb against its time cue before you tick true or false.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guests already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
They had already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
Nina is knowing every lyric in the musical.
I am used to cycling through the park in the rain.
We visited the science museum in March.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — The departure happened first, so past perfect is needed: "had already left."

Tip: When two past events stack, mark the earlier one with past perfect.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly shows that leaving preceded the trolley’s arrival.

Tip: "Already" often sits comfortably with past perfect in sequenced past narratives.

FALSE — Stative "know" resists continuous form; use "knows."

Tip: Mental-state verbs (know, believe, own) rarely take -ing in exam English.

TRUE — "Be used to" + gerund correctly means "accustomed to" a recurring activity.

Tip: "Am/is/are used to + -ing" ≠ "used to + V1."

TRUE — Past simple with "in March" correctly places a finished outing in a closed time frame.

Tip: Closed past time → past simple is the safe default.
tasks.solution_overview: This set contrasts past simple with past perfect, tests a stative continuous trap, and separates "used to" habit from "be used to" familiarity. Match the verb form to the timeline before you decide.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach has changed the starting line-up yesterday evening.
By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will pack our bags.
She has been a library volunteer here in 2016.
This scarf is belonging to my grandmother.
We used to camp by the lake before the path flooded.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Yesterday evening" is finished time, so write "changed," not present perfect.

Tip: Present perfect hates explicit finished-time adverbs.

FALSE — Completion before a future ferry arrival needs future perfect: "will have packed," not plain "will pack."

Tip: "By the time + future" often invites "will have + past participle."

FALSE — "In 2016" closes the period; use past simple: "was a library volunteer here in 2016."

Tip: "In + year" usually blocks present perfect for a finished role.

FALSE — "Belong" is stative; prefer "belongs," not continuous.

Tip: Possession and membership verbs stay simple in formal exam prose.

TRUE — "Used to camp" correctly reports a discontinued past habit.

Tip: "Used to + base verb" = past habit that no longer holds.
tasks.solution_overview: Only one sentence survives here. Hunt finished-time clashes with present perfect, demand future perfect with "by the time," and reject stative continuous — the lone survivor is clean past habit with "used to."

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The gallery has displayed local artists since the renovation.
While the neighbours were gardening, a fox slipped through the fence.
By year-end, the choir will have learned twelve new pieces.
Children used to play outdoors until dusk in this street.
Omar is owning three vintage cameras.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect + "since" correctly links an ongoing practice to its start point.

Tip: "Since" points to a start that still matters now — present perfect territory.

TRUE — Continuous background plus simple interrupt is the standard past pairing.

Tip: Ask which action was "in progress" when the other struck.

TRUE — Future perfect places learning completion before year-end.

Tip: Deadlines with "by" love future perfect.

TRUE — "Used to play" correctly describes a past habit that has changed.

Tip: Preferences and habits both take "used to + V1."

FALSE — Stative "own" should be "owns," not continuous.

Tip: Ownership verbs almost never take continuous in exam English.
tasks.solution_overview: Four sentences are clean; only the stative continuous fails. Confirm "since," background continuous, future perfect with "by," and past habit before you hunt the ownership trap.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The weather presenter explained the storm path at last week's briefing.
Runners are used to training before sunrise in winter.
The club has published three newsletters this semester.
By Friday noon, the caterers will have prepared the picnic baskets.
When the teacher entered, the class had already finished the quiz.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past simple correctly anchors a finished talk to "last week."

Tip: Explicit past time → past simple is rarely wrong.

TRUE — "Are used to training" correctly means runners are accustomed to the routine.

Tip: "Be used to + -ing" = familiarity, not past habit.

TRUE — Present perfect fits an unfinished period ("this semester") with present relevance.

Tip: "This week / this year / this semester" often keep present perfect alive.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places preparation before Friday noon.

Tip: Clock deadlines with "by" are classic future-perfect cues.

TRUE — Past perfect shows the quiz ended before the teacher walked in.

Tip: Earlier past action → had + past participle.
tasks.solution_overview: All five lines are sound. Use this card as a model set: closed past time, "be used to," unfinished-period present perfect, future perfect with "by," and past perfect sequencing.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I have seen that documentary twice already this month.
They are believing the rumours about the new café.
By dawn, the rescue team will have reached the ridge.
Sam used to hate spicy food, but now he loves it.
We are knowing each other since primary school.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "already" and an unfinished month fits repeated experience with present relevance.

Tip: "Already / yet / so far" often pair with present perfect.

FALSE — "Believe" is stative here; write "believe," not continuous.

Tip: Opinion verbs (believe, think = opinion) stay simple in careful English.

TRUE — Future perfect places arrival before dawn.

Tip: "By + future point" → will have + V3.

TRUE — "Used to hate" correctly marks a past taste that no longer holds.

Tip: Contrast "used to" with a present change to show discontinued habit.

FALSE — "Know" is stative and needs present perfect for a continuing relationship: "have known," not "are knowing."

Tip: Duration with "since" → present perfect simple for stative verbs.
tasks.solution_overview: Three survivors, two stative continuous fails. Trust present perfect for unfinished time, future perfect for "by," and "used to" for abandoned habits — then reject -ing on believe and know.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Priya has lived in Lisbon for six years.
The trail was still wet when we have arrived.
I am used to the noise from the tram line.
He used to be afraid of public speaking.
By the time the concert starts, we will have found our seats.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect + "for + duration" correctly shows a situation that continues now.

Tip: "For + length of time" with present perfect = still true.

FALSE — A completed arrival in a past narrative needs past simple: "when we arrived," not present perfect.

Tip: Do not mix a past continuous/simple story with present perfect for the same closed past.

TRUE — "Be used to" + noun correctly means accustomed to something.

Tip: After "be used to," a noun or -ing form both work.

TRUE — "Used to be" correctly describes a past state that has changed.

Tip: "Used to + be + adjective" is fine for former feelings or identities.

TRUE — Future perfect places finding seats before the concert begins.

Tip: "By the time + present" for future reference still wants will have in the main clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Watch the one timeline clash: a finished past arrival cannot wear present perfect. Everything else — "for," "be used to," "used to be," and future perfect — is clean.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery closed early last Sunday because of the heatwave.
She has just baked a loaf of sourdough.
Tom is preferring tea to coffee these days.
We will have walked ten kilometres by lunchtime.
My cousins used to visit us every summer.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Past simple with "last Sunday" correctly closes a finished event.

Tip: Day/date anchors → past simple.

TRUE — Present perfect with "just" marks a recent action with present relevance.

Tip: "Just / already / yet" are classic present-perfect companions.

FALSE — "Prefer" is stative; write "prefers," not continuous.

Tip: Likes and preferences stay simple unless you force a temporary "acting" sense (rare in exams).

TRUE — Future perfect correctly projects distance covered before lunchtime.

Tip: Distance or quantity "by" a future point → will have + V3.

TRUE — "Used to visit" correctly reports a repeated past habit.

Tip: Frequency phrases (every summer) sit naturally with "used to."
tasks.solution_overview: Four good lines and one stative continuous. Separate closed past ("last Sunday") from recent present perfect ("just"), then reject "is preferring."

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Did you ever climb a volcano?
Have you ever climbed a volcano?
While I was reading on the balcony, it started to snow.
They are used to get up early for rowing practice.
By next winter, she will have completed her first marathon.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Life experience up to now needs present perfect: "Have you ever climbed…?" Past simple "Did you ever" is non-standard in careful exam English for open experience.

Tip: "Ever" for lifetime experience → Have you ever + V3?

TRUE — Present perfect correctly asks about experience at any time up to now.

Tip: "Ever / never" + present perfect = life experience.

TRUE — Past continuous background + past simple interrupt is textbook.

Tip: Reading was in progress; snow was the interrupt.

FALSE — Familiarity needs "be used to" + -ing: "are used to getting up," not "are used to get."

Tip: After "be used to," add a gerund or a noun — never a bare infinitive.

TRUE — Future perfect places marathon completion before next winter.

Tip: "By next + season/year" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Compare the two experience questions side by side, keep the continuous–simple pair, fix "be used to" + -ing, and lock future perfect with "by next winter."

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app update has crashed twice since midnight.
I was understanding the lecture until the fire alarm rang.
We used to take the coastal path before the landslide.
By eight o’clock, the photographer will have set up the lights.
Hana has known her climbing partner for a decade.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect with "since midnight" fits repeated crashes still relevant now.

Tip: Tech glitches with "since" stay in present perfect.

FALSE — "Understand" is stative; use "understood" (past simple) for the background sense before the alarm.

Tip: Stative verbs rarely take past continuous in exam answers.

TRUE — "Used to take" correctly marks a discontinued route habit.

Tip: Past habit blocked by a later change → used to + V1.

TRUE — Future perfect places set-up before eight o’clock.

Tip: Clock "by" + future perfect.

TRUE — Present perfect of stative "know" with "for" correctly shows a continuing relationship.

Tip: "Have known … for" beats "am knowing."
tasks.solution_overview: Four keepers and one stative continuous. Trust "since," "used to," future perfect, and "have known" — reject "was understanding."

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: When we reached the summit, the sun has already risen.
When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen.
She is seeming tired after the long rehearsal.
I am getting used to the new keyboard layout.
They will have reheated the soup by the time you arrive.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Both events are in the past; the earlier sunrise needs past perfect, not present perfect.

Tip: Closed past narrative → had + V3 for the earlier action.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly places sunrise before the summit arrival.

Tip: "Already" + past perfect marks the prior completed state.

FALSE — "Seem" is stative; write "seems," not continuous.

Tip: Appearance verbs (seem, appear = look like) stay simple.

TRUE — "Get used to" + noun correctly means becoming accustomed.

Tip: "Get used to" = the process of adapting; "be used to" = already adapted.

TRUE — Future perfect places reheating before your arrival.

Tip: "By the time you arrive" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Contrast the two summit lines carefully, reject stative "seeming," and accept "get used to" plus future perfect as clean.

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: How long are you waiting for the night bus?
How long have you been waiting for the night bus?
The river flooded the towpath three times last winter.
Jonas used to living near the botanical gardens.
By Thursday evening, we will have curated the exhibition labels.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — Duration up to now with "how long" needs present perfect continuous: "have you been waiting."

Tip: "How long …?" for ongoing action → have/has been + -ing.

TRUE — Present perfect continuous correctly asks about waiting that started earlier and continues.

Tip: Visible temporary activity + duration → present perfect continuous.

TRUE — Past simple with "last winter" correctly counts finished floods in a closed season.

Tip: Numbered past events in a finished period → past simple.

FALSE — Past habit needs "used to live," not "used to living."

Tip: Never put -ing after "used to" for habit.

TRUE — Future perfect places curation before Thursday evening.

Tip: Art-deadline "by" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Duration questions need present perfect continuous, closed seasons need past simple, and "used to" never takes -ing for habit. Future perfect with "by" stays solid.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I have been meaning to call you all week.
This jacket is fitting me perfectly today.
We had finished dinner before the guests rang the doorbell.
She is used to cook for large family gatherings.
By the time the podcast drops, the host will have recorded three more episodes.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — Present perfect continuous of "mean" is an accepted fixed pattern for delayed intention.

Tip: "Have been meaning to…" is a rare continuous that exams often accept.

FALSE — "Fit" as a size/state is stative; prefer "fits" (or "fit" in AmE past) — not continuous for a permanent/current size fact.

Tip: Clothing size → simple: It fits me.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly shows dinner ended before the doorbell.

Tip: "Before" often helps you spot the earlier past action.

FALSE — Familiarity needs "is used to cooking," not "is used to cook."

Tip: Be used to + -ing / noun, never bare infinitive.

TRUE — Future perfect places recording before the podcast release.

Tip: Media schedules with "by the time" invite will have.
tasks.solution_overview: Accept the idiomatic "have been meaning," keep past perfect and future perfect, and reject stative "fitting" plus the bare infinitive after "be used to."

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Since moving abroad, Lara is making friends more easily.
Since moving abroad, Lara has been making friends more easily.
The museum used to open only on weekdays.
I am tasting the soup to check the seasoning.
By noon tomorrow, the drones will have mapped the whole coastline.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Since" with a continuing change needs present perfect (continuous), not present continuous alone.

Tip: "Since + -ing / since + time" → have/has (been) + verb.

TRUE — Present perfect continuous correctly links the move to an ongoing social change.

Tip: Process + since → have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Used to open" correctly reports a former schedule.

Tip: Former rules and timetables take used to + V1.

TRUE — "Taste" here is a deliberate action (sampling), so continuous is allowed.

Tip: Dynamic sense of sense verbs (taste/smell/feel on purpose) can take -ing.

TRUE — Future perfect places mapping completion before noon tomorrow.

Tip: Science deadlines with "by" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Pair the "since" lines carefully, keep "used to" and future perfect, and notice when a sense verb becomes dynamic ("am tasting") so continuous is fine.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He has gone to the allotment — he should be back by dusk.
He has been to the allotment three times this week.
We are loving this new pottery class.
They will have been travelling for fourteen hours by the time they land.
I used to be used to the cold winters, but I am not any more.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "Has gone" correctly means he went and is still away.

Tip: Has gone = left and not back yet.

TRUE — "Has been to" correctly means visited and returned (experience/count).

Tip: Has been to = visited; has gone to = still there.

FALSE — In careful exam English, "love" stays stative: "We love this class," not continuous (marketing "I’m loving" is informal).

Tip: Exam default: like/love/hate → simple forms.

TRUE — Future perfect continuous correctly stresses duration before landing.

Tip: "By the time" + duration → will have been + -ing.

TRUE — The sentence deliberately contrasts "used to be" (past state) with "be used to" (familiarity) — both forms are used correctly.

Tip: Used to be ≠ be used to; you can combine them when meaning requires it.
tasks.solution_overview: Master "gone" versus "been," reject informal continuous "loving," accept future perfect continuous for duration, and parse the double "used to" contrast carefully.

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This is the first time I have ever tried paddleboarding.
This is the first time I ever tried paddleboarding.
While the barista was frothing milk, the espresso machine jammed.
People are depending on the coastal path for weekend walks.
By the end of the festival, performers will have given forty shows.
tactical_explanations:
TRUE — "This is the first time" requires present perfect for the new experience.

Tip: First/second/third time + present perfect.

FALSE — Past simple after "this is the first time" breaks the pattern; use "have ever tried."

Tip: If the sentence starts with "This is the first time," expect have/has + V3.

TRUE — Continuous background + simple interrupt works for café chaos too.

Tip: Machine jam = short interrupt.

TRUE — "Depend" here describes a current community pattern; continuous is acceptable for a temporary/current reliance (and simple "depend" would also work).

Tip: Some verbs allow continuous when you stress a current situation.

TRUE — Future perfect totals shows before the festival ends.

Tip: Quantity completed "by the end" → will have + V3.
tasks.solution_overview: Lock the "first time" + present perfect rule, keep the café interrupt pair and future perfect, and treat "are depending" as an acceptable current-situation continuous.

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have packed a warmer coat yesterday.
I wish I had packed a warmer coat yesterday.
She has been working on the mural all morning and still isn’t finished.
The soup is smelling of garlic and thyme right now.
By next spring, we will have been volunteering at the shelter for five years.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — After "I wish" for a past regret, use past perfect: "I wish I had packed," not "would have packed."

Tip: Wish + past perfect for past regrets; save would for present wishes about others’ behaviour.

TRUE — Past perfect correctly expresses a regret about yesterday’s packing.

Tip: I wish + had + V3 = past counterfactual.

TRUE — Present perfect continuous correctly stresses ongoing unfinished mural work.

Tip: All morning + still going → have been + -ing.

TRUE — "Smell" here reports a temporary sensory impression, so continuous is natural.

Tip: Dynamic sense (how something smells now) can take continuous; stative "It smells of garlic" is also fine.

TRUE — Future perfect continuous correctly projects five years of volunteering completed by next spring.

Tip: Duration up to a future point → will have been + -ing.
tasks.solution_overview: Fix the wish-regret pattern, then accept present perfect continuous, a dynamic sensory continuous, and future perfect continuous for long-running volunteering.

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: It’s high time we have updated the club website.
It’s high time we updated the club website.
After the storm had passed, birds began singing again.
I am seeing what you mean about the plot twist.
They will finish the crossword by tonight — in fact, they will have finished it by six.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "It’s high time" takes a past-simple form with present meaning: "updated," not present perfect.

Tip: High time / about time + past simple (unreal present).

TRUE — Past simple after "It’s high time" correctly marks overdue action.

Tip: Treat "high time" like a mini-unreal: past form, present urgency.

TRUE — Past perfect for the earlier storm, past simple for the later singing — clean sequence.

Tip: After + past perfect, then simple past for the next event.

TRUE — "See" here means "understand," and continuous "am seeing" is accepted in modern careful English for gradual understanding (simple "see" is also fine).

Tip: Mental "see" can take continuous when understanding unfolds.

TRUE — The second clause correctly upgrades to future perfect for a clearer "by six" completion.

Tip: "Will finish by" is ok; "will have finished by" is more precise for completion.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the "high time" + past simple rule, keep past-perfect sequencing, accept gradual "am seeing," and prefer future perfect for precise "by" completion.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No sooner the train had left than the platform announcement began.
No sooner had the train left than the platform announcement began.
I have yet to try the new climbing wall downtown.
We are having a brilliant time at the street festival.
By the time you read this postcard, we will already arrive in Lisbon.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "No sooner" needs inversion: "No sooner had the train left…," not subject–verb order without the auxiliary fronted.

Tip: No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than…

TRUE — Inverted past perfect correctly pairs with "than" for immediate sequence.

Tip: Inversion after no sooner / hardly / scarcely is exam gold.

TRUE — "Have yet to" is a present-perfect pattern meaning "still haven’t done."

Tip: Have yet to + V1 = still outstanding.

TRUE — "Have" for experiences/enjoyment is dynamic, so continuous is fine.

Tip: Having a good time / having lunch = action; owning = stative.

FALSE — "By the time" with a future reading needs future perfect: "will already have arrived," not "will already arrive."

Tip: By the time + present → will have + V3 in the main clause.
tasks.solution_overview: Force inversion after "no sooner," keep "have yet to" and dynamic "having," and repair the broken future perfect after "by the time."

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Hardly I had sat down when my phone buzzed.
Hardly had I sat down when my phone buzzed.
She has been wanting a pottery wheel for months.
I’m thinking that the gallery closes too early on Mondays.
In two hours’ time, the tide will have turned and the rock pools will be underwater.
tactical_explanations:
FALSE — "Hardly" needs inversion with past perfect: "Hardly had I sat down…"

Tip: Hardly / scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when…

TRUE — Correct inverted past perfect for an immediate follow-up event.

Tip: Match hardly … when with had + V3 after the fronted adverb.

TRUE — "Want" occasionally takes present perfect continuous for a long-standing desire; this is accepted in modern exam-tolerant English.

Tip: Have been wanting = desire lasting up to now.

FALSE — Opinion "think" (= believe) is stative: "I think that…," not "I’m thinking that…" Continuous "thinking" is for mental process ("I’m thinking about a title").

Tip: Think = opinion → simple; think about = considering → continuous ok.

TRUE — Future perfect correctly places the turn of the tide before the two-hour mark, with a clear present-result consequence.

Tip: Nature deadlines with "in … time" + will have work well.
tasks.solution_overview: Close with inversion after "hardly," accept long-running "has been wanting," reject opinion continuous "I’m thinking that," and keep future perfect for the tide.
